title: Lowland Whisky Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What Lowland Scotch whisky is, where the region sits, why it tastes light and grassy and how to taste it against bigger malts.
teaser: Lowland malts are the quiet ones in the Scotch family. Quiet is not the same as simple.
standfirst: The Lowlands cover the south of Scotland, below the old Highland Line. The malts made there are known for a light, grassy, floral style that suits a beer drinker's palate well. Here is what shapes that style and how to taste it properly.
sections: The Lowlands are defined by a line on the map

Scotch whisky has five protected regions: Highland, Lowland, Speyside, Campbeltown and Islay. The Lowland region is everything south of the Highland Line, the boundary that runs roughly from Greenock on the Clyde to Dundee on the Tay. Edinburgh and Glasgow both sit inside it.

The region is a place of origin, not a recipe. A Lowland malt still follows every rule that makes a whisky Scotch: at least three years in oak casks in Scotland and a minimum of 40% ABV in the bottle. Our guide to what makes a whisky Scotch covers those rules in full. What the region tells you is a tendency, not a guarantee.
Light, grassy and floral is the house style

Ask a whisky writer to describe a classic Lowland malt and you will hear the same words: cut grass, lemon peel, green apple, honeysuckle, a soft biscuity malt note underneath. Most are unpeated or very lightly peated, so smoke rarely gets in the way.

For a beer drinker the comparison is a pale lager against an imperial stout. The Lowland style is the pale lager end of malt whisky. The flavours are delicate, which means they are also easy to drown with ice, a heavy glass or a cask that was too active.
Triple distillation is part of the story

Most Scotch malt is distilled twice in copper pot stills. The Lowlands have a long tradition of distilling three times. At least one well-known Lowland distillery still triple distils its whole output.

Each extra distillation strips out heavier compounds and pushes the spirit to a higher strength off the still. Double distilled new make spirit usually comes off the spirit still at around 68 to 72% ABV on average. Triple distilled spirit can reach around 80% ABV or more. The result is a cleaner, lighter new make with fewer of the oily, sulphury notes that give some Highland and island malts their weight.

Not every Lowland distillery triple distils, so treat it as a regional habit rather than a rule.
The region shrank and then came back

The Lowlands once had many more working malt distilleries. Through the twentieth century most of them closed. For a long stretch only a handful were still running. The region was better known for its large grain distilleries, which make the column still spirit that goes into blended Scotch.

Since the 2000s a wave of new malt distilleries has opened across the south of Scotland. That matters for tasting: a newer distillery may bottle younger malts or take its spirit in a direction quite different from the old light style. Read the label and the age statement before you assume what is in the glass.

Young does not mean poor. A clean, well made three or four year old malt can be lively and fresh. It will simply taste more of the spirit and less of the cask than a 12 year old. Tasting young and older Lowland malts side by side is one of the clearest ways to learn what time in oak actually adds.
How cask choice shows through a light spirit

A delicate spirit hides nothing. Put it in a first fill ex-bourbon barrel and you get vanilla, coconut and soft toffee laid over the grass and citrus. Put it in a first fill sherry butt and the dried fruit can flatten the spirit completely.

That is why many classic Lowland bottlings lean on ex-bourbon and refill casks. Refill casks have already given up much of their colour and flavour to an earlier fill, so the spirit character comes through clearly. If you are learning to taste, a 10 or 12 year old Lowland malt from ex-bourbon casks is one of the cleanest windows onto what a distillery's spirit tastes like. Our guide to recognising bourbon cask character helps you separate the two.
Tasting a Lowland malt the right way

Use a tulip shaped glass, not a heavy tumbler. Pour about 25 ml. In an Indian summer, keep the bottle out of direct sun and pour in a cool room. At 32 °C the alcohol lifts out of the glass faster than the grassy top notes, so the whisky seems hotter and thinner than it is.

Nose it before any water. Then add a few drops, swirl and nose again. Light malts often open up with a little water because the floral esters are pushed out of the alcohol. Taste in small sips and hold each one briefly before swallowing. Drink water between pours and pace yourself. Never drink and drive.

The real lesson comes from comparison. A light Lowland malt next to a peated Islay malt shows you what the word light means far better than any tasting note can. Telling green apple from pear or honeysuckle from heather is a trained skill, not a gift.
Start with one bottle and one comparison

Your first step is simple. Buy or share one Lowland single malt, ideally around 10 to 12 years old from ex-bourbon casks. Taste it beside a Speyside malt you already know. Write down three aromas for each, then compare your lists. The words that appear on one list but not the other are the Lowland style, described in your own language.
faqs: Where is the Lowland whisky region?
It covers the south of Scotland, below the Highland Line that runs roughly from Greenock to Dundee. Edinburgh and Glasgow both fall inside it.
Are all Lowland whiskies triple distilled?
No. Triple distillation is a Lowland tradition and some distilleries still do it, but many Lowland malts are double distilled like most other Scotch.
What does Lowland whisky taste like?
Typically light and fresh: cut grass, citrus, green apple, flowers and soft malt. Most are unpeated.
Is Lowland whisky good for beginners?
Often, yes. Its lighter body and lack of smoke make it an easy starting point, especially for drinkers who prefer pale beers.
